2027-07-30.title: Friday of the Seventeenth Week in Ordinary Time · St Peter Chrysologus
readings: These are the appointed festivals of the Lord, the holy convocations
Sing with joy to God our help
Prophets are not without honor except in their own country and in their own house
2027-07-30.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 17 (Year I). The first reading begins the festival calendar of Leviticus, read today and tomorrow. The optional memorial of St Peter Chrysologus, bishop and doctor of the Church, may be kept (liturgical colour white); if it is not kept, green. Psalm verses are given in NRSV numbering.
2027-07-30.verse: And they took offense at him. But Jesus said to them, “Prophets are not without honor except in their own country and in their own house.” And he did not do many deeds of power there, because of their unbelief.
theo: The Book of Leviticus opens a calendar. “These are the appointed festivals of the Lord, the holy convocations, which you shall celebrate at the time appointed for them.” Time itself becomes holy. The year of Israel is not a mere wheel of seasons, but a series of meetings with God at fixed hours. First comes the Passover, “on the fourteenth day of the month, at twilight,” followed by seven days of unleavened bread, the memorial of the night of the Exodus. Then the first fruits: when the harvest begins, the people bring “the sheaf of the first fruits” to the priest, who raises it before the Lord “on the day after the sabbath.” From that day they “count off seven weeks... fifty days,” and then bring an offering of new grain, the feast of Weeks, which Greek-speaking Jews called Pentecost, “the fiftieth.” Then the Day of Atonement, “you shall deny yourselves,” when the people confessed their sins, and the Feast of Booths, seven days of living in huts of branches in memory of the wilderness. These festivals are God's gifts to Israel, and the Jewish people still keep them with faithfulness; the Church honours them as such and teaches that God's covenant with Israel has never been revoked (Nostra Aetate 4; Catechism 839). Christians also see in them a pattern that was fulfilled in Christ. He died at Passover; he rose on “the day after the sabbath,” which is the day of the first fruits, and St Paul calls him “the first fruits of those who have died” (1 Corinthians 15:20); fifty days later the Holy Spirit came at Pentecost. The Psalm is the song for such feasts: “Sing aloud to God our strength; shout for joy to the God of Jacob. Raise a song, sound the tambourine, the sweet lyre with the harp. Blow the trumpet at the new moon, at the full moon, on our festal day. For it is a statute for Israel.”

In the Gospel Jesus comes “to his hometown” of Nazareth and teaches in the synagogue. The people are astounded, but their astonishment does not turn into faith. “Where did this man get this wisdom and these deeds of power? Is not this the carpenter's son? Is not his mother called Mary? And are not his brothers James and Joseph and Simon and Judas? And are not all his sisters with us?” They know everything about him except who he is. The “brothers” and “sisters” are, in the language of the Bible, close relatives; the Church has always taught that Mary remained a virgin and that Jesus was her only child (Catechism 499–500). “They took offense at him”: the Greek word means that he became a stumbling block to them. Familiarity can hide holiness; they could not believe that God could be so near, so ordinary, so well known. Jesus answers with a proverb: “Prophets are not without honor except in their own country and in their own house.” Then St Matthew says something sobering: “he did not do many deeds of power there, because of their unbelief.” God does not force his gifts on anyone; where faith is closed, there is little the Lord can do. The two readings belong together. In Leviticus God comes near on the appointed days, and the people have to be ready to meet him. In Nazareth he came near on an ordinary day, in an ordinary man, and they missed him. We should be careful that we do not miss him either, in the Mass we know so well, in the neighbour we think we know, in the daily bread of our own home. St Peter Chrysologus, whom the Church remembers today, was a bishop who knew how to make the familiar words of the Gospel sound new.
outline: Ask: what is so familiar to you in your faith that you no longer see it?
God sets appointed feasts, and meets his people at fixed hours.
Passover, the sheaf, the fifty days: and Christ the first fruits of the dead.
Familiarity blinds: they took offense, and the Lord could do little for their unbelief.
“Prophets are not without honor except in their own country and in their own house.”
live: Choose one rhythm of holy time and keep it faithfully this week: Sunday Mass without hurry, a short daily prayer at the same hour, or the first Friday devotion.
At the next Mass, ask the Lord to let you see Jesus as if for the first time, and greet someone you take for granted with fresh attention.
saints: Born at Imola, Archbishop of Ravenna from about 433 until his death. He was called Chrysologus, “golden word,” because of his short, clear and warm sermons, about 180 of which survive. He taught that prayer, fasting and mercy are one: “Prayer knocks at the door, fasting obtains, mercy receives” (Sermon 43, in substance). Pope Benedict XIII declared him a doctor of the Church in 1729. His memorial, 30 July, is optional.
2027-07-30.prayer: O God, who made Saint Peter Chrysologus an outstanding preacher of your incarnate Word, grant, we pray, that we may always ponder in our hearts the mystery of your salvation, which he so wonderfully expounded, and faithfully express it in the way we live. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord, you come near to us on the appointed days and on the plainest days. Open our eyes, so that we may recognise you in the Mass, in the Word and in our neighbour, and keep us from the unbelief of those who knew you too well to know you. Amen.
altar: Israel's feasts were meetings with God at an appointed time. The Mass is the meeting that Christ himself appointed: “Do this in remembrance of me.” It is not new each day, and that is both its strength and its risk, for we may come to it like the people of Nazareth, who thought they knew all about him. Before Communion the priest holds up the host and says: Behold the Lamb of God. Let us look at him as for the first time. The first fruits of the harvest of the dead is there on the altar, risen and giving himself.

quick: The Lord appoints the festivals of Israel: Passover, first fruits, the fifty days, the Day of Atonement and Booths.
In Nazareth the people are astounded by Jesus' wisdom but take offense at him, because they think they know him.
Jesus does not do many deeds of power in Nazareth because of the people's unbelief.
2027-07-30.action: Go to Mass or pray today as if you were meeting Jesus for the first time.
2027-07-30.question: What familiar part of my faith am I no longer seeing, and how can I look at it again?
kidsaint: Peter was a bishop in a city called Ravenna in Italy, a long time ago. He was a wonderful preacher, but he did not give long sermons. His sermons were short, clear and full of lovely pictures, so people loved to listen. They called him Chrysologus, which means golden word. He taught that prayer, fasting and kindness to the poor belong together. Lesson: a few good words, said with love, are worth more than many long ones.

family.explain: Jesus went back to Nazareth, where he had grown up, and taught in the synagogue. People were amazed, but then they said: he is only the carpenter's son! We know his mother and his family. They did not believe in him, and Jesus did not do many miracles there. Sometimes we think we know someone very well and we forget how special they are. Let us look at each other, at our parish and at the Mass with new eyes!
family.intention: We thank God for the feasts and Sundays that fill the year with joy, and we pray for people who have stopped believing.
family.ask: Ask: “What do we do on Sundays and feast days that makes them special? What could we do to make them more joyful?”

illus: An old sacristan in a church in Kottayam district had opened the same door at five o'clock every morning for forty years. A young visitor asked him whether he was tired of it. He said: some mornings I almost forget why I am doing it. And then I think that he is there, in the tabernacle, waiting for me as he was waiting for my father and my grandfather, and I feel as if I am opening the door for the first time. He said it was the one thing he prayed for: never to take the open door for granted. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: Lord of holy time, you come near on appointed days and on ordinary days. Open our eyes to know you. Amen.
share: These are the appointed festivals of the Lord (Leviticus 23:4). Which of the Church's feasts and seasons helps me most to meet him?
Where did this man get this wisdom? (Matthew 13:54). What in my faith have I stopped seeing because it is so familiar?
He did not do many deeds of power there, because of their unbelief (Matthew 13:58). Where might my own unbelief hold back what the Lord wants to do?
pm.resp: Sing with joy to God our help.
interc: For the Church, that she may keep the feasts with joy and welcome Christ afresh each day.
For the Jewish people, who keep the appointed festivals of the Lord, that they may be blessed in the covenant God has made with them.
For preachers and teachers, that like St Peter Chrysologus they may speak the Word with clarity and warmth.
For those who have grown tired of their faith, or taken the Lord for granted.
For our group, that we may meet the Lord with fresh eyes.
pm.close: Father, you give your people times and seasons to meet you. Make us ready to welcome your Son, who comes in the ordinary and the holy. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, Leviticus gives Israel a calendar of meetings with God: the Passover, the first fruits, the fifty days, the Day of Atonement, the Feast of Booths. These are the appointed festivals of the Lord (Leviticus 23:4). Time itself becomes holy. The Church too has a calendar: Sunday, Easter, Pentecost, the feasts of the saints. Why? Because we forget. We need fixed hours and seasons to remind us that God is near.

And God is faithful to those hours. At Passover the Lord rescued his people. The sheaf of first fruits is raised before him on the day after the sabbath, and we know what rose on that day: Christ, the first fruits of those who have died (1 Corinthians 15:20). Fifty days later came Pentecost. The festivals of Israel are God's gifts to the Jewish people, who keep them to this day, and in them we Christians see a pattern fulfilled in Christ. The Psalm says: Sing aloud to God our strength. Joy is the proper response.

But now look at the Gospel. Jesus goes to his hometown, and in the synagogue he teaches. People are astonished. Where did this man get this wisdom? Then comes the great but: is not this the carpenter's son? Is not his mother called Mary? They took offense at him (Matthew 13:57). They knew all about him, and they did not know him. And Matthew says: he did not do many deeds of power there, because of their unbelief.

How easily this happens to us. We have heard the Gospel a hundred times. We know the Mass by heart. We have seen the crucifix on the wall since we were children. And so we can sit in church and see nothing. Prophets are not without honor except in their own country and in their own house. Let us pray today for fresh eyes. St Peter Chrysologus, the golden-worded bishop, used to preach short sermons about the oldest passages of the Gospel and people would listen as if they had never heard them before. May the Lord give us that same freshness at the next Mass, when he will be in front of us again, on the altar, risen, the first fruits of our harvest. Amen.
kids: Children, a long time ago God told the people of Israel to have special feast days, when they would stop work and sing and thank him. We have feast days too, like Sundays and Christmas and Easter. In the Gospel Jesus went back to the village where he grew up, and the people said: he is only the carpenter's son! They did not see how special he was, so Jesus did not do many miracles there. Do not forget how special your family and friends are. And remember how special Jesus is every Sunday at Mass!

intro: Theme: “Prophets are not without honor except in their own country and in their own house.”
God's appointed feasts, Christ the first fruits, and the Nazareth that did not recognise him: holy time and fresh eyes.

sub: The appointed festivals of the Lord.
God meets his people at fixed hours.
q: These are the appointed festivals of the Lord, the holy convocations, which you shall celebrate at the time appointed for them.
But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, in order to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as children.
points.apply: Keep one fixed time of prayer every day this week, and make it a meeting, not a task.

sub: The sheaf raised on the day after the sabbath.
Fifty days to the new grain.
Christ the first fruits of the dead.
q: When you enter the land that I am giving you and you reap its harvest, you shall bring the sheaf of the first fruits of your harvest to the priest.
But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the first fruits of those who have died.
points.apply: Offer to God the first fruits of your week: the first minutes of the morning, the first share of your income, the first act of kindness.

sub: Is not this the carpenter's son?
Not many deeds of power, because of unbelief.
q: The stone that the builders rejected has become the chief cornerstone.
He came to what was his own, and his own people did not accept him. But to all who received him, who believed in his name, he gave power to become children of God.
points.apply: At Mass this week, look at the host with the eyes of someone seeing Jesus for the first time, and receive him with faith.

concl: God appoints times to meet his people, and in Christ the first fruits of the harvest of the dead the festivals find their fulfilment.
In Nazareth familiarity closed their eyes; the Lord asks us for the faith that sees him in the ordinary.
2027-07-30.resolve: Keep a fixed time of prayer each day this week, and look at the Mass and your neighbours with fresh eyes.
